To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the baseline expression of MRP in ES cells confers a protective role against multiple chemotherapeutic and toxic agents.

the MRP gene product is capable of conferring resistance to multiple drugs and that this resistance is mediated in part by the ability of this gene product to decrease intracellular drug accumulation.
the MRP gene is expressed in wild-type W9 ES cells and that double knockout of the MMR gene leads to increased sensitivity to chemotherapeutics and natural toxins.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the normal physiological function(s), if any, of MRP.
the role of the MRP protein in protecting the cell from the toxic effects of chemotherapeutic drugs.
the elucidation of the normal physiological functions of MRP and the role of this gene in the development of resistance to anticancer agents in tumor cell lines.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MRP is an important drug resistance mechanism, but its physiological role remains unclear.
MRP is not essential for the viability of ES cells, but its overexpression may contribute to drug resistance.
the baseline expression of MRP has the capacity to confer a protective role against a wide variety of chemotherapeutic drugs, but the physiological function(s) of MRP in the cell remain(s) unknown.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the MRP gene is a major determinant of drug resistance in embryonic stem cells.
the MRP gene is a major determinant of the sensitivity of ES cells to the toxicity of a wide variety of chemotherapeutic drugs.
MRP expression is not required for normal ES cell development in vitro, but it does play an important role in protecting cells from the toxic effects of a variety of drugs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
MRP1 is not the only MRP isoform capable of conferring resistance to chemotherapeutic agents.
the MRP gene product plays a protective role against a variety of toxic agents in the mouse embryo.
MRP1 is a major contributor to resistance to etoposide and teniposide.
